text.p: Sterling maintained its new-found strength across the board against the mark and the dollar, following the release of a slew of UK statistics which analysts said would have positive implications for a stronger pound.

"The UK data are stronger than expected and should underpin the rise in the pound. (They) highlight the relative outperformance of the UK economy versus continental Europe and will add to speculation that the next move in rates is up," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America in London.
At 0908 GMT sterling was trading in Europe at 2.4432/37 marks, off a 21-month high of 2.4475 which it hit overnight and against Tuesday's close of 2.4375/80.

Against the dollar, the pound was trading at $1.5852/61 against Tuesday's close of $1.5822/32. The pound remained bullish against the U.S. currency despite a half-a-cent drop overnight on the back of short-term profit taking after recent days of inexorable rises. Sterling's trade-weighted index against a basket of currencies was 88.8 against its previous close of 88.6, a rise of 5.7 percent since the start of August.
In the past week alone, sterling's rise against its trade-weighted basket has been a remarkable 1.8 percent.

Wednesday's UK data showed a greater-than-expected fall in unemployment during September to 35,600 for a jobless rate of 7.4 percent, while August average earnings rose an underlying 4.0 percent. September PSBR was a higher-than-expected 3.41 billion sterling.

Analysts said the figures showed little scope for any easing in fiscal or monetary policy, and employment minister Eric Forth said althouth the figues were on the high side, the government saw no signs of overheating.

Dealers said they expected sterling sentiment to remain bullish, thanks to its relative isolation from the growing debate over European economic and monetary union (EMU) and worries that the nascent euro might be a softer currency that central bankers would want.
Technical analysts said sterling's recent leap was not yet over and medium-term targets were now moving into focus.

"We have to go quite some way to find resistance...the first resistance level I'm focusing on is 2.45 (marks), which we have already been testing," said Geert-Jan Nikken, technical analyst at ABN AMRO in Amsterdam. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 6721
